title: Can Nature Benefit You If You’re Already Well? - Nautilus
gist: A Q&A framed around Roger Ulrich's 1984 landmark study (garden-view hospital patients healed faster with fewer complications) and E.O. Wilson's biophilia hypothesis sets up the question of whether nature exposure benefits people who are already healthy, not just the sick or stressed; the retrieved text ends before the neuroscientist's answer.

insights.claim: Roger Ulrich's landmark 1984 Science study found that hospital patients recovering from gallbladder surgery healed about a day faster, needed less pain medication, and had fewer post-surgical complications when their hospital room window looked out on a garden rather than a brick wall.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Foundational evidence base cited across healthcare design, biophilic architecture, and wellness real estate investment theses.
insights.locator: In 1984, Swedish healthcare design pioneer Roger Ulrich

insights.claim: E.O. Wilson's 1984 book Biophilia proposed that humans have an innate, evolutionarily derived tendency to seek connection with nature and other living things.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: The biophilia hypothesis underpins the broader biophilic-design and nature-based wellness product category.
insights.locator: That same year, biologist E.O. Wilson

insights.claim: The piece raises an open question of whether nature exposure provides measurable benefit to people who are already healthy and resilient, not just to the sick or stressed, but the retrieved text cuts off before the neuroscientist interviewee answers it.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: An open research question worth tracking: if nature exposure benefits the already-well, it broadens the addressable market for nature-based wellness interventions beyond clinical/recovery settings.
